paper_title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: In data-oriented recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Yin et al., 2025; Min et al., 2026), agents construct training data for their own subsequent learning and can jointly generate tasks and verification functions that provide reinforcement learning rewards (Zhou 1https://verifierbench.github.io/ 2https://huggingface.co/datasets/Catherine1213/VerifierBench 1 et al., 2026). These verifiers judge candidate solutions, determining which receive rewards or enter the training data. An incorrect verifier can therefore repeatedly reward violation or discard valid solution, making the reliability of agent-generated verifiers critical to this learning process. To examine this reliability, we study verifier generation (Zhang et al., 2025; Dinella et al., 2022): given the instruction and environment solver would receive, an agent writes an executable verifier that returns PASS or FAIL for any candidate solution. Unlike solver, which needs one valid solution, verifier must accept all valid solutions while rejecting invalid ones. It must therefore distinguish task requirements from choices that can vary across valid solutions. Figure 2 shows verifier rejecting permitted read-only query because the agent omits its tool from an allowlist. The selftests omit the same query and never establish that complete valid solution passes. verifier that accepts one expected solution may still reject other valid ways to complete task, while one that catches ordinary mistakes may still accept solutions that exploit gaps in its checks. Evaluating verifier generation therefore requires testing both acceptance of valid alternatives and rejection of invalid solutions, including deliberate attacks. Prior work evaluates generated test assertions (Dinella et al., 2022), unit tests (Jain et al., 2025), issue-reproducing tests (Mündler et al., 2024), and executable specifications (Endres et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026). We extend this line of evaluation to agent task completion, where correctness can depend on tool interactions, resulting environment states, and code changes. To this end, we build VerifierBench: 222 tasks from six open-source agent benchmarks with 4,993 hidden test cases, comprising reference solutions, valid alternatives, ordinary errors, and attacks on verification. This design tests whether generated verifiers distinguish task success from failure across different ways of carrying out the same task. Reliable measurement also requires trustworthy evaluation labels. Because both the benchmarks source verifiers and our constructed test cases can contain errors, we audit them with Verifier4Verifier (V4V), six checks that include replay, repeatability, and mutation testing. Source verifiers that pass this audit serve as the reference verifiers. Evaluating 19 models in common harness and 17 further modelharness configurations, we report three findings. First, generated verifiers accept valid solutions less reliably than they reject invalid ones: as reported in Section 3.2, true positive rates range from 21.1% to 70.2%, whereas true negative rates range from 79.2% to 96.3%. Second, as analyzed in Section 3.4, these false rejections concentrate in all-reject verifiers, which return FAIL on every test case of their task and produce 87.996.0% of false rejections in the analyzed records. Third, in selected cases examined in Section 4, these verifiers impose checks that the task does not require, and the agents self-tests either exercise only solutions those checks allow or never confirm that any valid solution passes. We thus contribute benchmark and screening procedure for verifier generation in Section 2, together with an analysis in Section 5 that motivates testing generated verifiers on permitted variations, not only on chosen solution.

sections.title: 2.1 Task Formulation
sections.content: For task t, an agent receives the instruction and environment used for ordinary task solving, together with the verifiers input and output conventions summarized in Appendix A. harness, the agent framework that manages model calls, tool use, and the generation loop, runs the agent until it delivers an executable verifier (cid:98)Vt; the reference verifier and hidden test cases are withheld. During generation, the agent may run self-tests: it writes candidate solutions of its own and checks that its draft verifier returns PASS for intended positives and FAIL for intended negatives. Because the hidden test cases are withheld, self-tests are the agents only evidence about how its verifier behaves. After generation, we fix (cid:98)Vt and run it on every test case in the tasks suite Ct. Each test case holds one candidate solution and carries reference label defined in Section 2.3, PASS for positive case and FAIL for negative one, which the verifier never sees. tool-call verifier receives raw call text together with parsed function names and arguments; state verifier receives the candidates interaction record or, for AppWorld, its solution code; and code verifier receives the candidate patch and repository checkout. For state and code tasks, both the generating agent and the delivered verifier can execute code in the task environment through public interface, run_public, for example to replay candidates actions or run repositorys tests. Executions during generation are budgeted separately from those during evaluation, as documented in Appendix E.

sections.title: 2.2 Task Sources and Test Cases
sections.content: We draw tasks from open-source agent benchmarks with executable evaluation procedures, each supplying an instruction, an environment, and source verifier. As summarized in the top of Table 1, toolcall tasks check called functions and arguments, state tasks check interactions or the resulting environment state, and code tasks check proposed software changes. Each test case receives construction label, PASS or FAIL, assigned from the task requirements and the change made to the solution before any verifier is run. As listed in the bottom of Table 1, test cases form four groups: the designated reference solution (gold); valid variants, which change presentation, implementation, or execution path while still satisfying every requirement; ordinary errors, namely initial outcomes, partial solutions, near misses, and regressions; and attacks, which exploit checking omissions, fabricate success signals, or interfere with verification. Valid variants test whether verifier accepts more than one expression of correct solution. Appendix details the nine construction categories behind these groups.

sections.title: 2.3 Screening with Verifier4Verifier
sections.content: These test cases are useful only if their labels are reliable. Construction labels and source verifiers can both be wrong: constructed case may not change the solution as intended, and source verifier may contain bugs. V4V applies six checks to the constructed test cases and source verifiers: 1. Replay. Run the source verifier on every test case and compare its decision with the construction label. 2 Figure 1: VerifierBench overview. Source tasks and source verifiers are combined with constructed test suites; V4V screens both, and the retained source verifiers become reference verifiers. The agent receives the instruction and environment used for ordinary task solving and generates one verifier, which is fixed before it is scored on multiple positive and negative test cases. Task: credit-card retention. Submit the requested card application and record the closure reason. Permitted tools include the read-only query get_user_dispute_history_7291. Generated check: The agent creates tool allowlist that omits this query and rejects unlisted operations. Self-tests during generation The intended-positive candidate omits the dispute-history query. The positive self-test returns FAIL: replay is unavailable after budget exhaustion. The agent acknowledges that positive validation is incomplete. Hidden positive test cases Valid candidates include the permitted dispute-history query. The verifier rejects the query as Unrelated or unsupported mutation. All 9 positive cases receive FAIL without environment execution. An incomplete allowlist excludes legal read; self-testing never confirms acceptance of complete valid solution. Figure 2: Overlooked task details lead to incorrect verification. The agents tool allowlist omits permitted read-only query, causing valid solutions to be rejected. Its self-tests omit the query and never confirm acceptance. GPT-6-astra with Claude Code on τ 2-bench banking task 044 rejects all 9 positive cases. 2. Repeatability. Rerun it on the same case from the same reset state; the decision must not change. 3. Provenance. Link every recorded decision to the test-case contents and verifier version that produced it. 4. Input-label consistency. Within task, cases that give the verifier identical information must not carry opposite labels. 5. Trivial baselines. Verifiers that always accept, always reject, or accept only the reference solution must be exposed by negative cases, positive cases, and valid variants, respectively. 6. Mutation testing. Modify one check in the source verifier (DeMillo et al., 1978); some test case must then receive different valid decisions from the two versions. We resolve any disagreement between construction label and source-verifier decision against the task requirements; agreement alone does not show that either is semantically correct. As detailed in Appendix B.1, confirmed source defects exclude 45 of the 267 initial tasks. All 37 Terminal-Bench tasks are removed, 35 of them because its test-output parser counts skipped tests as passes; the others are five BFCL tasks whose answer keys conflict with default-argument rules and three SWE-bench tasks with parsing and emptyreport errors. Defects in our own evaluation pipeline are corrected without excluding tasks. All 222 retained tasks pass the six checks, as reported in Appendix B.2, and their source verifiers become the reference verifiers . Because replay agrees on every test case, each construction label equals 3 the reference verifiers decision; we call this value the reference label and score generated verifiers against it.

sections.title: 2.4 Metrics
sections.content: A verifier invocation yields valid PASS, valid FAIL, or no valid decision (a missing verifier, timeout, crash, or malformed output). verifier that catches its own internal error and returns FAIL still yields valid decision, although it may not have completed its intended check. For each task, we compute the fraction of positive cases receiving PASS and the fraction of negative cases receiving FAIL; the true positive rate (TPR) and true negative rate (TNR) average these fractions across tasks, in percent. Our primary metric is normalized task-averaged balanced accuracy (Brodersen et al., 2010), which rescales BA = (TPR + TNR)/2 as BAnorm = 2 BA 100 = TPR + TNR 100. (1) It weights tasks equally and the two classes equally within each task. Constant valid decisions score 0 and perfect agreement scores 100; missing or invalid decisions stay in the denominators without credit. We also report the attack false-positive rate FPRh, the task-averaged fraction of attack cases that receive PASS. More results are in Appendices and G).

sections.title: 3.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models and harnesses. Our main comparison runs all 19 models in one common harness, Pi (Zechner, 2025). To measure how much the harness matters, we add 17 alternative configurations. They pair models with each familys native harness, the vendors own agent tool (Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025), Codex (OpenAI, 2025), or Gemini CLI (Google, 2025)), with the third-party harnesses OpenClaw (OpenClaw Foundation, 2026) and miniswe (Yang et al., 2024), and across families, as with GPT-6-astra in Claude Code. Because harnesses differ in prompts, tools, and reasoning settings, cross-harness comparisons describe configurations rather than model capability alone. Generation is limited to 5,400 seconds per task and 32,768 output tokens per reply, and every configuration is scored on all 222 tasks, as documented in Appendix E. Evidence sources. Our results draw on three sets of records. The main release holds the final judgments of all 36 configurations, and every reported score comes from it. The archived records are an earlier export with per-task judgments for nine Piharness models, whose aggregate counts match the main release, plus earlier verifier versions used in some appendix cases; the concentration analysis in Section 3.4 uses them. The Astra trace batch is separate generation of GPT-6-astra verifiers under four conditions, Pi or Claude Code at LOW or HIGH reasoning effort, that retains generation traces. It supports the effort comparison in Section 3.3 and the trace analysis in Section 4, and its scores never replace those of the main release.

sections.title: 3.4 Where False Rejections Concentrate
sections.content: These rates do not show whether false rejections are spread across tasks or repeated within the same task. We call verifier all-reject if it returns valid FAIL on every test case of its task, positive and negative alike. On that task its TPR is 0 and its TNR is 100, so it contributes zero to BAnorm, like constant decision. All-reject verifiers produce most false rejections. As Appendix Figure 5 shows, in the archived records they contribute 87.996.0% of each models positive FAIL decisions, whether test cases or tasks are weighted equally. The Astra trace batch reproduces the pattern, as reported in Appendix Table 22: in each condition, 6875 of the 222 verifiers are all-reject and contribute 93.395.5% of false rejections. The concentration of false rejections identifies where failures occur, but not why. BAnorm penalizes these failures but does not identify the checks responsible for them. We therefore inspect selected verifiers and their generation traces in Section 4.

sections.title: 4.1 Unjustified Checks
sections.content: Table 4 lists 16 verifiers from 12 tasks whose rejections we attribute to an unjustified check: condition that the instruction, tool definitions, and environment rules do not require, and that rejects solutions they permit. One such check can reject several positive cases of the same task. In τ 2-bench banking task 044, shown Tool calls. in Figure 2, the Claude Code/LOW verifier uses tool allowlist to exclude unrelated mutations but omits get_user_dispute_history_7291, permitted read-only query included in the public tool list. It treats this legal query as an unsupported mutation and rejects all nine positive cases before environment execution. The Pi/LOW verifier for 7 task 045 omits the same tool and also rejects all nine positives. Three other Pi/LOW verifiers (tasks 037, 040, and 041) reject authorized user-side calls or lack branch for them, rejecting another 27 positives without environment execution. Source files. Both Claude Code verifiers for Matplotlib-14623 exclude legal changes under lib/mpl_toolkits/, including the 3D axes implementation, and each rejects all four positive cases. Category vocabulary. In retail/34, the Claude Code/HIGH verifier identifies the tasks three office items with keyword list that omits Headphones, counts only two office items, and rejects all nine positive cases, as Appendix Figure 8 illustrates; two other HIGH-effort verifiers, for retail/33 and retail/34, share the omission. Representations. As detailed in Appendix I.2, the remaining verifiers accept only some permitted representations of value: an ISO-only currency format, numeric-only device identifiers, or incomplete decoding of TeX spacing.

sections.title: Challenging
sections.content: If these checks are visible in the generated code, why did self-testing not catch them? Table 4 splits the 16 verifiers by self-test outcome. For the eight in the upper block, the self-tests used only solutions that the unjustified check already In Django-11734, the positive self-test allows. patches query.py; the agent repairs subprocess compatibility, patch formatting, and environment resets until its positive and negative selftests return PASS and FAIL as intended, yet no self-test edits an __init__.py file. The passing Matplotlib self-tests modify other locations under lib/matplotlib/, such as axes/ _base.py and ticker.py, and the representation self-tests use only representations the checks accept. We call this confirmatory self-testing: the tests confirm that the verifier accepts chosen solution but never ask whether its other conditions follow from the task. More tests at the same permitted locations would not expose the restriction, and neither would negative self-tests: an invalid patch may violate genuine requirement while also tripping the unjustified check, so rejecting it correctly does not justify the check. As Appendix Figure 7 shows, Qwen3.7 Plus verifier exhibits the same pattern outside the Astra batch: it treats an omitted optional argument as empty instead of applying its documented default, and every positive self-test supplies that argument explicitly.

sections.title: 4.3 Self-Tests That Never Confirm Acceptance
sections.content: The eight verifiers in the lower block of Table 4 are the banking and retail verifiers of Section 4.1. Their agents ran intended-positive self-tests but never obtained complete positive PASS, as each agents final response acknowledges, so these runs do not establish acceptance even of the agents own intended solution. In the running example of Figure 2, the intended-positive self-test omits the permitted dispute-history query and fails when replay is unavailable after budget exhaustion; the tool restriction remains untested. At evaluation, the eight verifiers reject all 72 of their positive judgments without environment execution. Generation-time testing is constrained more broadly. Exploration and self-testing share one execution budget, which most HIGH-effort state and code runs exhaust as described in Section 3.3, and in two appendix traces shown in Appendix Figures 9 and 10 local execution fails because unshare is unavailable. These limits do not directly cause hidden rejections, since evaluation has its own budget, but they can leave verifiers checks unresolved when generation ends.

sections.title: Implications
sections.content: Self-testing generated verifier serves two goals: confirming that it accepts chosen solution, and checking that it does not reject other solutions the task allows. The second requires tracing every acceptance condition to the instruction, tool definitions, or environment rules, and testing it with cases derived from those requirements. One test varies permitted property while keeping the task satisfied, for example editing fields/__init__.py instead of query.py, omitting defaulted argument, or using an authorized user-side call; another violates one required condition. Examples drawn from solutions check already allows cannot challenge that check, and the Django configurations show that permitting legal source changes need not weaken rejection of tested violations. Testing must also be completed. Generation should reserve execution budget for testing the final verifier and should distinguish an execution failure from failed requirement: blocked test leaves its check unresolved, and repairing the execution does not validate checks the test never exercises. We do not evaluate the effectiveness of these directions.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Executable verifier generation. nl2postcond (Endres et al., 2024) and CodeSpecBench (Chen et al., 2026) generate executable specifications and evaluate them on valid and faulty behavior; CheckerBench (He et al., 2026) studies agentgenerated static-analysis checkers. We evaluate task-completion verifiers for tool-call, state, and code tasks, generated from the instruction and environment available for task solving. Test-oracle and test generation. TOGA (Dinella et al., 2022) generates test assertions, TestGenEval (Jain et al., 2025) evaluates unit-test generation, and SWTBench (Mündler et al., 2024) generates issuereproducing tests that also assess candidate patches. Our suites contain multiple valid variants and violations per task, and our trace analysis examines whether self-tests challenge unjustified checks. Automated training-data construction. Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2026) learns from selfproposed tasks with execution-based verification. Self-Challenging Language Model Agents (Zhou et al., 2026) jointly generates tasks, verification functions, and test examples for reinforcement learning. We hold tasks fixed to evaluate verifier generation in isolation, and identify errors that could affect which solutions enter training data.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: VerifierBench evaluates whether agents can write verifiers from the information available for solving task. Across all 36 configurations, generated verifiers accept valid solutions less reliably than they reject invalid ones, and in the analyzed records most false rejections come from verifiers that reject every case of their task. Code and trace inspection links these verifiers to unjustified checks and to selftests that either confirm only solutions those checks allow or never confirm acceptance at all. Verifier generation therefore needs tests that challenge each acceptance condition against the task requirements; otherwise, where generated verifiers select training data, as in data-oriented RSI, such checks could repeatedly exclude legitimate solution strategies.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Scores measure agreement with retained reference verifiers on finite, constructed test suites. As detailed in Appendix B, V4V excludes 45 tasks with confirmed source defects, but agreement between construction labels and reference decisions does not certify that every label is semantically correct. The 36 configurations differ in harness prompts, tools, and reasoning settings, so cross-harness differences describe configurations and do not isolate any harness component; rankings are point estimates without repeated generations or significance tests. The concentration analysis uses archived per-task records for nine models and the Astra trace batch for one model, rather than final per-task records for all 19 models. The code and trace analysis covers verifiers selected to explain observed failures, mostly from GPT-6-astra. It attributes rejections by inspecting source code rather than by intervention experiments, and it reads self-test outcomes from traces without reconstructing the verifier version at each self-test; it therefore identifies mechanisms but not their prevalence.

sections.content: The test suites contain 1,566 positive test cases (31.4%) and 3,427 negative test cases (68.6%). Table 10 describes the nine construction categories. The category records how test case was constructed and its intended positive or negative outcome; V4V checks the assigned label against the source verifier before the test suite is fixed. Neither category names nor labels are supplied during generation. In the main text, as grouped in Table 1, cosmetic and overstrict_trap cases together form the valid variants; base, partial, near_miss, and regression form the ordinary errors; and hack and process_violation form the attacks. For the six-group diagnostics, ordinary errors combine base, partial, near_miss, and regression (2,629 test cases). The remaining groups are reference solutions (222), cosmetic variants (840), alternative implementations or paths (504), hacks (796), and process violations (2). For the DNA-analysis task in Appendix I, those definitions state that mutation_type defaults to insertion; omitting that optional argument therefore preserves the requested operation. This explicit rule provides basis for identifying the generated verifiers incorrect treatment of the input. At evaluation time, the generated verifier receives candidate patch through diff field. The recorded generation process inspects the migration autodetector and runs the repositorys tests through the public execution tool. It then constructs behavior checks for the proposed patch and checks existing migration behavior. This instance demonstrates access to source code and executed tests, rather than reliance only on candidate-authored success report. It does not independently certify the retained reference or the integrity of every codetask environment.

sections.content: Table 24 compares GPT-5.6-sol, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3, all using the Pi harness, on one task of each type. Within each task, the models are evaluated on identical test-case contents. The comparisons use the archived records described in Section 3.1; they illustrate different failure mechanisms rather than explain the task-type rankings as whole. Input compatibility and omitted checks produce different errors. On ACE preference 17, GPT5.6-sol attempts to parse supplied profile string as structured data and rejects all six positives when parsing fails. Claude Opus 4.8 accepts all six positives but checks the requested location change without adequately checking preservation of the name and email, accepting 12 of 18 negatives. Kimi K3 checks these preserved fields and accepts only two negatives; both contain the same repeated-call payload, recorded in two construction categories. The comparison separates failure to interpret the supplied input from failure to enforce all required conditions. Early rejection can prevent state verification. On retail/34, GPT-5.6-sol requires tool result to parse as structured data before reaching its handling of bare user-ID string. The positive cases provide such string, so all nine receive FAIL before any environment replay. Claude Opus 4.8 and Kimi K3 handle this input and correctly judge all nine positives and eight negatives. This contrast identifies an input-processing failure, rather than an incorrect judgment of the resulting order state. Timeouts differ from incorrect decisions. On Django-11848, GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Opus 4.8 correctly judge all 15 test cases. Kimi K3 correctly judges nine, while one positive and five negatives time out. The records establish incomplete execution, but do not establish the cause of these timeouts. Together, the cases show why score differences require separate examination of input handling, task-specific checks, and completion of execution. I.2 Attributing Rejections to Unjustified

Its recorded generation includes test described as function call, constructed by placing JSON dictionary inside the functions parentheses. The test passes. The reference solution in the test suite instead expresses the arguments as Python keywords, including bookingId=R123. The generated parser extracts the text inside the parentheses and attempts to decode it with json.loads or ast.literal_eval. keyword-argument list is neither JSON value nor Python literal expression, so neither operation parses that text. The self-test passes because it uses precisely the representation accepted by the parser. The verifier input format provides raw and parsed call fields, but the generation prompt gives no concrete grammar for the raw field. This case supports input incompatibility and inadequate selftest coverage, rather than claim that the model ignored an explicit syntax requirement.
